_comment: Federal court orders about AI use in filings, maintained by hand. last_reviewed is set by hand only, to the date a person actually re-checked every source link below. Never auto-advance it (no workflow, script or build step may change it). If reviews stop, the page shows the old date as-is and the table is collapsed (legal/court-orders.js collapses it once last_reviewed is more than 21 days old) rather than shown as fresh. A row needs an official court source (a .uscourts.gov site or the court's own page/PDF); no official source means no row. After editing, run: python3 scripts/build_court_ai_orders.py
scope: Federal courts only (selected orders, not a complete list)
note: A list of court orders about AI use in filings, maintained by hand. It may be incomplete or out of date. Check the official source. Not legal advice.

rows.summary: A brief prepared using generative AI must say so on its first page under the heading "Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence"; a brief without that heading certifies that no AI was used.
A filer who used AI to prepare any paper must disclose that use and certify that every citation to the law or the record has been verified as accurate.
In consent cases, Rule 12 and Rule 56 motions, motions to amend, and opposed motions must include a certification on the use or non-use of generative AI; filings without it are stricken.

Every filing must contain a certification on the use or non-use of generative AI, stating that any AI-drafted language was reviewed by a person and that cited authority exists; noncompliant filings may be stricken.
Every filing must end with a certification that no generative AI was used, or that AI-drafted language was reviewed by a person and all citations are to real authority and reflect its contents.

All filings must include a "Certificate of Generative Artificial Intelligence Usage" stating whether AI was used, which tool, how it was used, and that the filer checked the accuracy of AI-assisted content.
Attorneys and pro se parties may not use AI to prepare any filing; the order says this does not cover legal or internet search engines such as Westlaw, LexisNexis, Google or Bing.

rows.court: U.S. District Court, D. New Mexico
rows.summary: A party who uses a generative AI tool to prepare a filing must disclose that use and the tool in the document and certify that AI-drafted portions, including citations, were checked for accuracy.
Filers must verify that any AI-generated language in a filing was checked for accuracy using print reporters, traditional legal databases, or other reliable means.
A filing prepared in any aspect with generative AI must come with a signed attestation that names the AI program and certifies that the document was checked for factual and legal accuracy.

Filers who use generative AI must ensure that citations and statements of fact are accurate and supported; the court may stop reviewing, deny, or dismiss a filing that contains a miscited or misrepresented citation or fact.
